result.summary: Menalcidas cheats Callicrates of his share of the Oropian bribe, and Callicrates has him prosecuted. Diæus, bribed, saves Menalcidas and lies to the Achæans about what the Roman Senate allowed, which brings war between the Achæans and Sparta. Both sides are deceived while the Roman ambassadors travel slowly.

scenes.title: Menalcidas cheats Callicrates
scenes.summary: The Oropians pay Menalcidas, who keeps all the money. Callicrates, angered, removes him from office and prosecutes him before the Achæans.
scenes.stakes: Menalcidas risks his office and his life on a capital charge; Callicrates loses his share of the bribe.

scenes.title: Diæus lies about the Senate
scenes.summary: Menalcidas bribes Diæus, who gets him acquitted. Diæus then misreports the Senate's ruling to the Achæans, claiming they may pass death sentences on Spartans.
scenes.stakes: Sparta's right to appeal to Rome and its citizens' lives are at risk from Diæus's lie.

scenes.title: War threatens; exiles flee Sparta
scenes.summary: War breaks out and Diæus names 24 Spartans as culprits. Agasisthenes persuades them to go into exile, and they are condemned in absence.
scenes.stakes: The 24 Spartans risk death, and Sparta risks war with the Achæans.

scenes.title: Dispute before the Roman Senate
scenes.summary: Callicrates dies on the road. Diæus and Menalcidas quarrel before the Senate, and while the Roman ambassadors dawdle each deceives his own side.
scenes.stakes: Both peoples are misled about their standing, risking war and Roman anger.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses Lacedæmonians and Spartans for the same people.

notable_quotes.reason: A proverb-like verse mocking Menalcidas as worse in treachery than even Callicrates.

analysis.text: Bribery and deceit drive Greek politics toward ruin, as Pausanias shows leaders putting private gain above their cities.
The passage describes the run-up to the Achæan War of 146 BC, when Roman arbitration was shaping Greek affairs.

language_notes.text: The Oropians had been promised payment to Menalcidas for securing relief after Athens's raid on Oropus; Achæan help never came, yet they still had to pay.
The 'proverb' is a mock-proverb in verse style, using stock comparisons from nature to say Menalcidas surpassed even Callicrates in treachery.
'Viz.' is an abbreviation of Latin videlicet, meaning 'namely'; it introduces the specific charges.
'Capital charge' means a charge punishable by death.
'Debateable land' means territory whose ownership was disputed between Sparta and another state.
'Without common consent' means member cities needed approval of the whole League before sending their own embassy to Rome.
Lacedæmonians is another name for the Spartans; Lacedæmon is the region and city of Sparta. The text uses both names interchangeably.
"All that troubled her" is Diæus's pretext: he claims to attack only Sparta's troublemakers, not the city itself, which lets him justify war.
"Nominally tried" means the trial was only a formality; the exiles were absent and the verdict was a foregone conclusion.
"Decorous" means proper and dignified; the quarrel was therefore undignified and heated.
"Jurisdiction" means legal authority; Menalcidas claims Sparta had been freed from the Achæan League's authority.

context_notes.text: Talents were large units of money by weight of silver; three talents was a substantial bribe.
Rome's Senate was by now the arbiter of Greek disputes, and Greek states competed to gain its favour.
The Achæan League was a federation of Greek cities, each bound to follow the orders of the League's elected general.
Rome was by now the arbiter of Greek disputes, so both sides appealed to the Roman Senate.

literary_notes.text: The mock-proverb ironically praises Menalcidas by comparison, making the notoriously treacherous Callicrates look honest.
The narrator openly states that Diæus lied, guiding the reader's judgment of his corruption.
Pausanias interjects his own speculation, a characteristic personal aside; he muses on whether Callicrates' death spared the Achæans harm or good.
The Roman envoys' slow journey, "somehow" so leisurely, gives both rivals time to spread lies; the delay quietly sharpens the coming disaster.
